blocks.body:
How big is a function? The largest value it takes is one answer; the area under $|f|$ is another; the energy $\int|f|^2$, which appears in physics and in Fourier analysis, is a third. Each choice turns a space of functions into a [[normed-spaces|normed space]], and the family of choices $\big(\int|f|^p\big)^{1/p}$, indexed by $1 \le p \le \infty$, gives the $L^p$ spaces.

They are complete, which the Riemann-integrable functions are not; $L^2$ is a Hilbert space, the natural home of Fourier series and quantum mechanics; and the inequalities of Hölder and Minkowski that hold in them are the basic tools for estimating integrals in PDE, harmonic analysis and probability. This page assumes the [[lebesgue|Lebesgue integral]] on a measure space.

blocks.title: First impressions: the p-norms
blocks.body:
Start with vectors. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put $\|x\|_p = \big(\sum|x_i|^p\big)^{1/p}$ and $\|x\|_\infty = \max|x_i|$. For $x = (3,4)$:

$$\|x\|_1 = 7,\quad \|x\|_2 = 5,\quad \|x\|_3 = 91^{1/3} \approx 4.498,\quad \|x\|_\infty = 4.$$

The norms decrease in $p$ and tend to the largest coordinate. In the plane the unit ball $\{\|x\|_p \le 1\}$ is a diamond for $p = 1$, a disc for $p = 2$, and a square for $p = \infty$, with rounded squares in between.

For functions, $p$ decides which kind of bad behaviour is penalised. On $(0,1]$, the function $x^{-a}$ (with $a > 0$) has $\int_0^1 x^{-ap}\,dx < \infty$ exactly when $ap < 1$: large $p$ punishes tall spikes. On $[1,\infty)$, $\int_1^\infty x^{-ap}\,dx < \infty$ exactly when $ap > 1$: small $p$ punishes slow decay. So on a finite interval, $L^p$ shrinks as $p$ grows; on $\mathbb{R}$ neither space contains the other.

blocks.title: Lᵖ spaces
blocks.body:
Let $(X, \mathcal{M}, \mu)$ be a measure space and $1 \le p < \infty$. For measurable $f : X \to \mathbb{C}$ set

$$\|f\|_p = \Big(\int_X |f|^p\,d\mu\Big)^{1/p}, \qquad \|f\|_\infty = \inf\{M \ge 0 : |f| \le M \ \mu\text{-almost everywhere}\}$$

(the essential supremum). For $1 \le p \le \infty$, $L^p(X,\mu)$ is the set of measurable $f$ with $\|f\|_p < \infty$, where two functions are identified if they agree $\mu$-almost everywhere. For counting measure on $\mathbb{N}$ one writes $\ell^p$.

The identification is not pedantry: $\|f\|_p = 0$ means only that $f = 0$ almost everywhere, so without it $\|\cdot\|_p$ would not be a norm. Elements of $L^p$ are equivalence classes; their values at individual points are not defined.

blocks.title: Hölder's inequality
blocks.body:
Let $1 < p < \infty$ and let $q$ be the conjugate exponent, $\frac1p + \frac1q = 1$ (also $p = 1$, $q = \infty$). For measurable $f, g$,

$$\int_X |fg|\,d\mu \le \|f\|_p\,\|g\|_q.$$

For $1 < p < \infty$ and $\|f\|_p, \|g\|_q$ finite and non-zero, equality holds if and only if $|f|^p$ and $|g|^q$ are proportional almost everywhere. The case $p = q = 2$ is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

First Young's inequality: for $a, b \ge 0$, $ab \le \frac{a^p}{p} + \frac{b^q}{q}$, with equality iff $a^p = b^q$. If $a$ or $b$ is $0$ this is clear. Otherwise, since $\log$ is strictly concave ([[convexity]]),

$$\log\Big(\frac{a^p}{p} + \frac{b^q}{q}\Big) \ge \frac1p\log a^p + \frac1q\log b^q = \log(ab),$$

with equality iff $a^p = b^q$.

The case $p = 1$, $q = \infty$ is immediate from $|fg| \le |f|\,\|g\|_\infty$ a.e. For $1 < p < \infty$: if $\|f\|_p = 0$ or $\|g\|_q = 0$ then $fg = 0$ a.e. and both sides vanish; if either is infinite there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, by homogeneity we may scale so that $\|f\|_p = \|g\|_q = 1$. Apply Young pointwise with $a = |f(x)|$, $b = |g(x)|$ and integrate:

$$\int|fg|\,d\mu \le \frac1p\int|f|^p\,d\mu + \frac1q\int|g|^q\,d\mu = \frac1p + \frac1q = 1 = \|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$

Equality forces equality in Young almost everywhere, i.e. $|f|^p = |g|^q$ a.e. (after the scaling), which is the stated condition.

blocks.title: Minkowski's inequality
blocks.body: For $1 \le p \le \infty$ and $f, g \in L^p$, $\|f + g\|_p \le \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p$. Consequently $\|\cdot\|_p$ is a norm on $L^p$.

The cases $p = 1$ and $p = \infty$ follow from $|f + g| \le |f| + |g|$. Let $1 < p < \infty$. First, $L^p$ is closed under addition, since $|f + g|^p \le (2\max(|f|,|g|))^p \le 2^p(|f|^p + |g|^p)$. Now write $|f + g|^p \le |f|\,|f+g|^{p-1} + |g|\,|f+g|^{p-1}$ and apply Hölder to each term with exponents $p$ and $q = p/(p-1)$, noting $\big\||f+g|^{p-1}\big\|_q = \|f+g\|_p^{p-1}$:

$$\|f+g\|_p^p \le \big(\|f\|_p + \|g\|_p\big)\|f+g\|_p^{p-1}.$$

If $\|f + g\|_p = 0$ there is nothing to prove; otherwise divide by $\|f+g\|_p^{p-1}$.

blocks.title: Riesz–Fischer theorem
blocks.body: For every measure space and every $1 \le p \le \infty$, $L^p(X,\mu)$ is complete, hence a Banach space. Moreover, if $f_n \to f$ in $L^p$ with $p < \infty$, some subsequence converges to $f$ almost everywhere.

We treat $p < \infty$ (the case $p = \infty$ is a uniform-convergence argument off a null set). A normed space is complete if every absolutely convergent series converges: given a Cauchy sequence, choose $n_1 < n_2 < \cdots$ with $\|f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k}\| < 2^{-k}$; the telescoping series $f_{n_1} + \sum_k (f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k})$ is absolutely convergent, its sum is the limit of the subsequence, and a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges.

So let $g_k \in L^p$ with $\sum_k\|g_k\|_p = S < \infty$. Put $G_n = \sum_{k \le n}|g_k|$ and $G = \sum_k|g_k|$ (with values in $[0,\infty]$). By Minkowski, $\|G_n\|_p \le S$, and by monotone convergence $\int G^p = \lim\int G_n^p \le S^p$. So $G < \infty$ a.e., and on that set the series $\sum g_k(x)$ converges absolutely, to $F(x)$ say. Since $|F| \le G$, $F \in L^p$. Finally $|F - \sum_{k \le n}g_k|^p \le (2G)^p$, which is integrable, and the left side tends to $0$ a.e., so by dominated convergence $\|F - \sum_{k\le n}g_k\|_p \to 0$.

The a.e. statement comes out of the same argument: the subsequence $f_{n_k}$ chosen above converges a.e. to the limit, since the telescoping series converges absolutely a.e.

blocks.title: L² is special; how the spaces compare
blocks.body:
Only one of these spaces carries an inner product compatible with its norm. $L^2$ has $\langle f, g\rangle = \int f\bar g\,d\mu$ with $\langle f,f\rangle = \|f\|_2^2$, so with Riesz–Fischer it is a [[hilbert-spaces|Hilbert space]], with orthogonal projections and orthonormal bases. For $p \ne 2$ the parallelogram law $\|f+g\|^2 + \|f-g\|^2 = 2\|f\|^2 + 2\|g\|^2$ fails (see the example below), so no inner product induces $\|\cdot\|_p$.

How the spaces sit together:

- If $\mu(X) < \infty$ and $p < q$, then $L^q \subseteq L^p$ with $\|f\|_p \le \mu(X)^{1/p - 1/q}\|f\|_q$ (apply Hölder to $|f|^p \cdot 1$ with exponents $q/p$ and its conjugate).
- For sequences the inclusion goes the other way: $\ell^p \subseteq \ell^q$ for $p < q$, with $\|x\|_q \le \|x\|_p$.
- In general, if $p < q < r$ and $\frac1q = \frac\theta p + \frac{1-\theta}{r}$, then $\|f\|_q \le \|f\|_p^{\theta}\|f\|_r^{1-\theta}$. So $L^p \cap L^r \subseteq L^q$, and $\log\|f\|_{q}$ is a convex function of $1/q$.
- If $\mu(X) < \infty$ then $\|f\|_p \to \|f\|_\infty$ as $p \to \infty$.

blocks.title: Density, duality, and beyond
blocks.body: For readers continuing to functional analysis. Simple functions are dense in $L^p$ for every $p$ (integrable simple functions when $p < \infty$), and for $p < \infty$ the continuous functions with compact support are dense in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. This last fact fails for $L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$, which is not even separable. For $1 \le p < \infty$ (and $\sigma$-finite $\mu$ when $p = 1$), every bounded linear functional on $L^p$ has the form $f \mapsto \int fg\,d\mu$ for a unique $g \in L^q$, so the dual of $L^p$ is $L^q$; for $1 < p < \infty$ this makes $L^p$ reflexive, whereas $L^1$ and $L^\infty$ are not (apart from finite-dimensional cases). Hölder's inequality and its equality case give $\|f\|_p = \sup\{|\int fg| : \|g\|_q \le 1\}$ for $1 \le p < \infty$, which together with [[hahn-banach]] is how many estimates are proved. The Riesz–Thorin theorem interpolates bounds for linear operators between $L^p$ spaces, giving for instance the Hausdorff–Young inequality for the [[fourier-transform]], and Sobolev spaces, built from functions whose derivatives lie in $L^p$, are the setting for the modern theory of PDE.

blocks.title: Which p? Spikes versus tails
blocks.body: (a) For which $p \in [1,\infty]$ is $f(x) = x^{-1/3}$ in $L^p(0,1)$? Compute $\|f\|_p$ when it is finite. (b) For which $p$ is $g(x) = x^{-1/3}$ in $L^p(1,\infty)$? (c) Find a function on $(0,\infty)$ that lies in $L^p$ for exactly one $p$.
blocks.solution:
(a) $\int_0^1 x^{-p/3}\,dx$ is finite iff $p/3 < 1$, i.e. $p < 3$, and then equals $\frac{1}{1 - p/3} = \frac{3}{3-p}$, so $\|f\|_p = \big(\frac{3}{3-p}\big)^{1/p}$. For instance $\|f\|_1 = 3/2$ and $\|f\|_2 = \sqrt3$. $f$ is unbounded, so $f \notin L^\infty$. Answer: $1 \le p < 3$.

(b) $\int_1^\infty x^{-p/3}\,dx < \infty$ iff $p > 3$; also $g \le 1$, so $g \in L^\infty$. Answer: $3 < p \le \infty$.

(c) Glue the two behaviours at the borderline: take $h(x) = x^{-1/2}\big(1 + |\ln x|\big)^{-1}$. Substituting $x = e^{u}$ turns $\int_0^\infty |h|^p\,dx$ into $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{u(1 - p/2)}(1+|u|)^{-p}\,du$. If $p \ne 2$ the exponential factor blows up at one end, so the integral diverges; if $p = 2$ it is $2\int_0^\infty (1+u)^{-2}\,du = 2$. So $h \in L^p(0,\infty)$ exactly for $p = 2$ (and $h \notin L^\infty$ since it blows up at $0$).

blocks.title: Hölder with the equality case
blocks.body: Find the largest possible value of $\int_0^1 x f(x)\,dx$ over measurable $f \ge 0$ with $\int_0^1 f^3\,dx = 1$, and a function attaining it.
blocks.solution:
Hölder with $p = 3$ and $q = 3/2$ gives

$$\int_0^1 x f(x)\,dx \le \|f\|_3\,\|x\|_{3/2} = 1\cdot\Big(\int_0^1 x^{3/2}\,dx\Big)^{2/3} = \Big(\frac25\Big)^{2/3} \approx 0.5429.$$

Equality requires $f^3$ proportional to $x^{3/2}$, i.e. $f = c\sqrt x$. The constraint $\int_0^1 c^3x^{3/2}\,dx = \frac{2c^3}{5} = 1$ gives $c = (5/2)^{1/3}$. Check: $\int_0^1 x\cdot c\sqrt x\,dx = \frac{2c}{5} = \frac25\Big(\frac52\Big)^{1/3} = \Big(\frac25\Big)^{2/3}$. So the maximum is $(2/5)^{2/3}$.

blocks.title: Two structural facts
blocks.body: (a) Show that the parallelogram law fails in $L^p[0,1]$ for every $p \ne 2$. (b) Show that $\|f\|_p \to \|f\|_\infty$ as $p \to \infty$ when $\mu(X) < \infty$, and check it for $f(x) = x$ on $[0,1]$.
blocks.solution:
(a) Let $f = \mathbf{1}_{[0,1/2]}$ and $g = \mathbf{1}_{(1/2,1]}$. Then $|f + g| = |f - g| = 1$, so $\|f+g\|_p^2 + \|f-g\|_p^2 = 2$, while $2\|f\|_p^2 + 2\|g\|_p^2 = 4\cdot 2^{-2/p}$. These are equal iff $2^{-2/p} = 1/2$, i.e. $p = 2$. (For $p = \infty$ the right side is $4$.)

(b) Let $M = \|f\|_\infty$. For any $p$, $\|f\|_p \le M\mu(X)^{1/p} \to M$, so $\limsup\|f\|_p \le M$. For $\varepsilon \in (0, M)$, the set $A = \{|f| > M - \varepsilon\}$ has positive measure by definition of the essential supremum, and $\|f\|_p \ge (M - \varepsilon)\mu(A)^{1/p} \to M - \varepsilon$. So $\liminf\|f\|_p \ge M - \varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon$. (If $M = \infty$, the second argument with any finite level shows $\|f\|_p \to \infty$.)

For $f(x) = x$: $\|f\|_p = (p+1)^{-1/p}$, which is $1/2$ at $p = 1$, $1/\sqrt3 \approx 0.577$ at $p = 2$, about $0.955$ at $p = 100$, and tends to $1 = \|f\|_\infty$.

blocks.title: A three-term Hölder inequality
blocks.body:
Prove that for positive reals $a_i, b_i, c_i$ ($i = 1, \dots, n$),

$$\Big(\sum_i a_ib_ic_i\Big)^3 \le \Big(\sum_i a_i^3\Big)\Big(\sum_i b_i^3\Big)\Big(\sum_i c_i^3\Big).$$
blocks.solution:
Apply Hölder on $\ell^p$ with $p = 3$, $q = 3/2$ to the sequences $(a_i)$ and $(b_ic_i)$:

$$\sum a_ib_ic_i \le \Big(\sum a_i^3\Big)^{1/3}\Big(\sum (b_ic_i)^{3/2}\Big)^{2/3}.$$

Apply Cauchy–Schwarz ($p = q = 2$) to $(b_i^{3/2})$ and $(c_i^{3/2})$: $\sum (b_ic_i)^{3/2} \le \big(\sum b_i^3\big)^{1/2}\big(\sum c_i^3\big)^{1/2}$. Substituting,

$$\sum a_ib_ic_i \le \Big(\sum a_i^3\Big)^{1/3}\Big(\sum b_i^3\Big)^{1/3}\Big(\sum c_i^3\Big)^{1/3},$$

and cubing gives the claim. The same argument proves $\int|f_1\cdots f_k| \le \prod\|f_j\|_{p_j}$ whenever $\sum 1/p_j = 1$.

blocks.body:
- Convergence in $L^p$ does not imply convergence almost everywhere. The typewriter sequence (indicators of $[0,1],[0,\tfrac12],[\tfrac12,1],[0,\tfrac13],[\tfrac13,\tfrac23],\ldots$) tends to $0$ in every $L^p$ with $p < \infty$, yet at every point it takes the value $1$ infinitely often. Only a subsequence converges a.e.
- Conversely, a.e. convergence does not imply $L^p$ convergence: $n\mathbf{1}_{(0,1/n)} \to 0$ everywhere on $(0,1)$ but has $L^1$ norm $1$. Dominated convergence is the usual bridge.
- For $0 < p < 1$ the formula $(\int|f|^p)^{1/p}$ is not a norm: with $f = \mathbf{1}_{[0,1/2]}$, $g = \mathbf{1}_{(1/2,1]}$ and $p = 1/2$, $\|f+g\| = 1$ but $\|f\| + \|g\| = 1/2$.
- Inclusions depend on the measure: $L^2 \subseteq L^1$ on $[0,1]$ but not on $\mathbb{R}$ (take $1/(1+|x|)$), and $\ell^1 \subseteq \ell^2$ for sequences.
- $L^\infty$ is the essential supremum: changing $f$ on a null set does not change it, and $\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}$ has $\|\cdot\|_\infty = 0$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

$L^p$ spaces are the main examples of [[normed-spaces|Banach spaces]], and $L^2$ is the model [[hilbert-spaces|Hilbert space]]: [[fourier-series]] converge in $L^2$ by Parseval, and the [[fourier-transform]] is an isometry of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ (Plancherel). Duality $(L^p)^* = L^q$ is a central application of the Radon–Nikodym theorem; integral operators with square-integrable kernels on $L^2$ are [[compact-operators]]. In probability, $L^p$ norms of [[random-variables]] are moments, $L^2$ convergence is mean-square convergence, and bounded families in $L^p$ ($p > 1$) are the uniformly integrable ones that [[martingales]] theory needs. Existence theory in the [[calculus-of-variations]] is set in Sobolev spaces built on $L^p$.

1. Show that if $\mu(X) = 1$ then $\|f\|_1 \le \|f\|_2 \le \|f\|_\infty$, and give an example on $[0,1]$ where both inequalities are strict.
2. Prove that $\ell^1 \subseteq \ell^2$ with $\|x\|_2 \le \|x\|_1$, and show that the inclusion is strict.
3. Let $f \in L^1(\mathbb{R}) \cap L^\infty(\mathbb{R})$. Prove that $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R})$ for every $1 \le p \le \infty$ and that $\|f\|_p \le \|f\|_1^{1/p}\|f\|_\infty^{1 - 1/p}$.
4. Prove that $L^\infty[0,1]$ is not separable by exhibiting uncountably many functions at pairwise distance $1$.
